title: Pericyclic reactions II
goal: Recognise retro, hetero, ene and cheletropic variants of the pericyclic reactions, draw hydrogen shifts and 8π closures, and use the Woodward–Hoffmann rules to say which are allowed.

problemSets.title: Cycloadditions and their relatives
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: The Diels–Alder ring of six electrons can run backwards, include a heteroatom, use a C–H bond or end on a single atom.
problemSets.conceptCard:
The cyclic arrows of the Diels–Alder reaction turn up in several disguises. Each is still one step with six electrons moving round a ring.

- **retro-Diels–Alder**: the cyclohexene unzips back into a diene and a dienophile. Heat and entropy (one molecule becomes two) drive it, especially when a product distils off or is very stable.
- **hetero-Diels–Alder**: a C=O or C=N is the dienophile, or a heteroatom sits in the diene. Very electron-rich dienes such as **Danishefsky's diene** add even to plain aldehydes; acid then turns the adduct into a dihydropyranone.
- **ene reaction**: one of the three pairs is an **allylic C–H σ bond**. A new C–C bond forms, the C=C shifts along, and the H moves to the enophile.
- **cheletropic reaction**: both σ bonds that form or break end on **one atom**. 3-Sulfolene loses SO₂ to give butadiene, a safe way to use a gas.

All of them are suprafacial on each partner and, where it applies, endo; the app does not check stereochemistry yet, so this is explained in the text.

setItems.whyThisOne: Cracking dicyclopentadiene: the Diels–Alder run backwards.
A C=O as the dienophile, then acid work-up to a dihydropyranone.
A C–H bond replaces one π bond in the ring of six electrons.
Two bonds break to one atom, and a gas leaves.

problemSets.title: Sigmatropic hydrogen shifts
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: An H moves along a π system, staying on one face: [1,5] shifts are allowed on heating, [1,3] are not.
problemSets.conceptCard:
In a **[1,j] hydrogen shift** an H leaves one carbon and bonds to the carbon *j* atoms along a π system, while the π bonds shift. Count the H as atom 1 of one fragment, the carbon it leaves as atom 1 of the other.

Which shifts happen on heating follows the electron count, like every pericyclic reaction:

- **[1,5]**: six electrons, **suprafacial** (the H stays on one face): allowed and common
- **[1,3]**: four electrons; it would have to be **antarafacial** (the H crossing to the other face), which a small H cannot reach: not seen
- **[1,7]**: eight electrons, antarafacial: allowed, because a long triene can twist into a helix

In 5-substituted cyclopentadienes a [1,5] shift runs even at room temperature, moving the H to the neighbouring ring carbon, so they must be kept cold. The app cannot yet offer that particular new bond (the H moving to the next ring atom), so this set draws an open-chain diene instead. Faces are explained in the text; the app does not check them.

setItems.whyThisOne: The allowed hydrogen shift: six electrons, one face.

problemSets.title: Selection rules
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: Count the electrons: 4n + 2 or 4n, heat or light, decides whether a pericyclic reaction is allowed and which way it turns.
problemSets.conceptCard:
The **Woodward–Hoffmann rules** in one line: a thermal pericyclic reaction is allowed when the number of (4q + 2)s and (4r)a components is **odd**. In practice, count the electrons that move:

- **4n + 2** (6, 10): on heating, all suprafacial; electrocyclic reactions **disrotatory**
- **4n** (4, 8): on heating, one component must be antarafacial; electrocyclic reactions **conrotatory**
- under **light** every rule swaps

So an (E,Z,Z,E)-octatetraene closes conrotatory (8π) to a trans-disubstituted cyclooctatriene, which then closes disrotatory (6π) to a bicyclo[4.2.0]octadiene. The app draws the first closure; the second makes a four-membered ring, a new bond the app cannot offer yet, so it is described in the text.

**Photochemistry comes later.** Light-driven reactions, such as the [2+2] cycloaddition of two alkenes to a cyclobutane or the Norrish type II cleavage of a ketone, go through excited states, which the app cannot draw yet. They will get their own problems once it can.

setItems.whyThisOne: Eight electrons close conrotatory: the 4n rule.

problemSets.title: Checkpoint
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: Find the ring of moving electrons, whatever it is disguised as.
problemSets.conceptCard: Reactions from every set, shuffled, names hidden until you finish. Three attempts per step.
